extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in algebra and number theory; instructors and readers studying classical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of classical proof techniques and structural arguments used to prove (a) existence of primitive elements in finite fields and Wedderburn's theorem, (b) irrationality results for e, π and related numbers, and (c) evaluations of ζ(2)=π^2/6 using integral and trigonometric methods. The page gives lemmas, constructions, and bounding strategies used in these proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting elements of given order in finite fields (ψ(d) vs ϕ(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ψ(d) = #{ b ∈ F* : ord(b) = d }. If ord(b) = d then b, b^2, ..., b^d=1 are roots of x^d − 1, and ord(b^i) = d/(i,d). Hence ord(b^i)=d iff (i,d)=1, so ψ(d)=ϕ(d) whenever ψ(d)>0; counting reduced fractions shows ∑_{d|n} ϕ(d) = n and forces ψ(d)=ϕ(d) for all d, in particular giving an element of order n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the root-count of x^d−1 in a field (at most d roots), the formula ord(b^i)=d/(i,d), and Euler's totient ϕ(d). The fraction-reduction/counting argument verifies ∑_{d|n}ϕ(d)=n and establishes existence of primitive n-th roots (generators) by ψ(n)=ϕ(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclotomic polynomials φ_d(x) have integer coefficients and constant ±1
rubrics_metrics.description: Group all complex n-th roots of unity of order d and set φ_d(x) = ∏_{λ of order d} (x − λ). Then x^n − 1 = ∏_{d|n} φ_d(x). The claim: φ_n(x) ∈ Z[x] and its constant coefficient is ±1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction on d using the factorization x^n − 1 = p(x) φ_n(x) where p(x)=∏_{d|n,d<n}φ_d(x). Comparing coefficients (equations (3) and (4)) and using that earlier φ_d(x) have integer coefficients and constant ±1 yields that φ_n(x) also has integer coefficients and constant ±1. This is the standard cyclotomic-polynomial integrality argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use integer-valued cyclotomic evaluations to get divisibility contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate φ_n(q) for an integer q (cardinality of center/field in Wedderburn argument) and deduce divisibility relations φ_d(q) | (q^n − 1) / (q^{n_k} − 1) from the class formula; combine with analytic size estimates on φ_n(q) to reach contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After establishing combinatorial/class-number divisibility constraints (from conjugacy class sizes and dimensions over center), show that φ_n(q) must divide a certain integer smaller than φ_n(q) (using magnitude bounds like |φ_n(q)| > q^something), yielding an impossibility. This completes proofs like Witt's proof of Wedderburn's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wedderburn/Witt proof structure via centralizers and class equation
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite division ring R with center Z of size q, regard R as a vector space over Z of dimension n (|R|=q^n). For s∈R, centralizer C_s is a sub-division ring with size q^{n_s}. Define conjugacy classes A_s = { x^{-1} s x : x∈R* } partitioning R*; use class equation grouping central elements Z* and nontrivial classes A_k to obtain formula (1): q^n − 1 = q − 1 + ∑_{k=1}^t (q^n − 1)/(q^{n_k} − 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic counting yields divisibility constraints q^{n_k} − 1 | q^n − 1 and further number-theoretic conditions (e.g., n_k | n). Combine these with cyclotomic polynomial facts (φ_d(q) integrality and size) to force a contradiction when R is assumed noncommutative, proving R is a field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct polynomial f(x) with integer coefficients and controlled size (lemma for irrationality proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed n≥1 define f(x) = x^n(1−x)^n / n! (or equivalently a polynomial of degree 2n with integer coefficients divided by n!). The lemma states: (i) f is a polynomial of the form ∑_{i=n}^{2n} c_i x^i with integer coefficients c_i; (ii) 0 < f(x) < 1/n! for 0<x<1; (iii) the derivatives f^{(k)}(0) and f^{(k)}(1) are integers for all k ≤ 2n (and related integrality properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specially chosen polynomial provides integer boundary values of certain derivative-linear combinations and a very small positive integral when integrated against exponential/trigonometric functions; these properties are the engine of Niven/Hermite-style irrationality proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Niven/Hermite method for proving e^s irrational using F built from f and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume e^s = a/b rational. Define F(x) as a linear combination of derivatives of f(x) with coefficients s^{2n}, s^{2n−1}, ...: F(x) = s^{2n} f(x) − s^{2n−1} f'(x) + ... + f^{(2n)}(x). Differentiate and form the identity d/dx[ e^{s x} F(x) ] = s^{2n+1} e^{s x} f(x). Integrate from 0 to 1 and use that F(0), F(1) are integers to deduce an integer N with 0 < N < 1, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose n large enough so that factorial bounds (n! > a s^{2n+1}) make the integral N strictly between 0 and 1, impossible for an integer. The structure relies on (i)-(iii) of the lemma for integrality and smallness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous construction to prove π^2 irrational via integration against sin(πx)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume π^2 = a/b rational and build F(x)= b n π^{2n} f(x) − b n π^{2n−2} f''(x) + ... so that F''(x) + π^2 F(x) = b n π^{2n+2} f(x). Use the identity (F'(x) sin πx − π F(x) cos πx)' = π^{2} b n f(x) sin πx and integrate from 0 to 1 to obtain an integer N = F(0)+F(1) that is positive but can be made <1 for large n, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This adapts the Hermite technique to second-order ODE structure and uses the lemma's integrality/bound properties. Choose n so π a n / n! < 1 to force the contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric/divisibility method for irrationality of (1/π) arccos(1/√n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ϕ_n = arccos(1/√n) with cos ϕ_n = 1/√n. Use the cosine addition formula cos((k+1)ϕ)=2 cosϕ cos kϕ − cos((k−1)ϕ) to inductively represent cos(kϕ_n) = A_k / √(n^k) with integers A_k not divisible by n. If (1/π)ϕ_n were rational (ℓϕ_n = kπ), then ±1 = cos(kπ) = A_ℓ/√(n^ℓ) forcing n | A_ℓ, contradiction for odd n≥3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an instance of using integer recurrence relations coming from trig addition formulas together with divisibility constraints to contradict rationality assumptions on certain normalized angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-integral method to evaluate ζ(2) = π^2/6
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider I = ∫_0^1 ∫_0^1 [xy / (1−xy)] dx dy. Expanding integrand as geometric series gives I = ∑_{n≥0} 1/(n+1)^2 = ζ(2). A change of variables (rotation and scaling or specific substitution) evaluates the same integral to π^2/6, yielding Euler's series value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First expand 1/(1−xy)=∑(xy)^n and integrate termwise to get the zeta series. Second, perform a coordinate transformation (e.g., u = (x+y)/√2, v = (y−x)/√2 or the Beukers-type substitution described) to evaluate the integral in closed form and equate the two evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beukers–Calabi–Kolk substitution for ζ(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the substitution u = arccos( x / √(1−x^2 y^2) ), v = arccos( y / √(1−x^2 y^2) ) (equivalently x = sin u / cos v, y = sin v / cos u) which maps the unit square (0,1)^2 bijectively to the triangle {u,v>0, u+v<π/2}. The Jacobian determinant equals 1/(1−x^2 y^2), so the integral reduces to the area of the triangle giving π^2/8 for the odd-only sum and hence π^2/6 overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the Jacobian explicitly (determinant simplifies to 1/(1 − x^2 y^2)). The transformed integral equals the triangle's area, giving an elegant geometric evaluation of the integral that matches the zeta-series evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cotangent-polynomial identity and inequalities method for ζ(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n=2m+1 form the polynomial whose roots are t_r = cot^2(rπ/(2m+1)) (r=1..m). From expansion of sin(nx) as polynomial in sin x and cos x one derives sum identities: ∑_{r=1}^m cot^2(rπ/(2m+1)) = 2m(2m+1)/6 and ∑ csc^2 = 2m(2m+2)/6. Using inequalities cot y < 1/y < csc y for 0<y<π/2 and summing yields bounds converging to π^2/6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive the polynomial via imaginary part of (cos x + i sin x)^n and compare coefficients to get the sum-of-roots identity. Apply elementary inequalities for cot and csc and let m→∞ to obtain the zeta value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate tails of series by comparison with integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: For bounding the remainder ∑_{n=m+1}^∞ 1/n^2 use integral comparison: ∑_{n=m+1}^∞ 1/n^2 < ∫_m^∞ dt/t^2 = 1/m and ∑_{n=m+1}^∞ 1/n^2 > ∫_{m+1}^∞ dt/t^2 = 1/(m+1). A slightly refined lower bound uses convexity to get 1/[2(m+1)].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives explicit quantitative control of convergence speed for ζ(2) partial sums; for instance, summing 10^6 terms yields an error on the order of 10^{-6} and explains observed digit accuracy patterns when truncating the series.
